sections.heading: EIP-8141 Frame Transactions Update
sections.summary: Frames spec changes over the past two months are mostly clarifications and Glamsterdam integration, especially explicit 2D gas support via EIP-8037.
sections.body:
- lightclient thanked Nethermind, ethrex, Steel, and Tomas for contributions to the Frame spec over the past two months.
- Changes fall into two buckets:
  - Clarifications that do not change implementation behavior but tighten the EIP language.
  - Integration of Glamsterdam changes, principally explicit two-dimensional gas (state gas via EIP-8037) in the transaction object, receipts, and handling.
- 2D gas is the most visible change since the signature list was added in May; it surfaces many small areas of previously undefined behavior that had to be specified.
- Other Glamsterdam integrations include removal of block refunds, data-flow pricing, and correct storage-refund counting within frames.
- Toni Wahrstätter reported ongoing work building privacy protocol proof-of-concepts on top of Frames, including a TornadoCash-style withdrawal sponsored by the pool itself (no relayer needed); an ethrex devnet for exploration already exists.
- Recent changes to EIP-8141 and its 4 PFI-to-Hegota dependents are tracked at [forkcast.org](https://forkcast.org/eips/8141/?tab=history) and [dependents tab](https://forkcast.org/eips/8141/?tab=dependents).
- lightclient noted that 2D nonce and recent roots are deliberately kept out of EIP-8141 itself because they are controversial L1 features; they can be layered on without blocking Frames.
  - Recent roots can be done out-of-protocol with a mempool rule (like expiry) and does not need an envelope change.
- The reason for not shipping pure frames and EIP-8288 together with 8141 was similarly to avoid blocking progress on contentious items.

sections.heading: EIP-8130 Presentation and L2 Adoption
sections.summary: Chris presented EIP-8130's decoupled authenticator/keystore model, noting Base targets late-September launch with OP Stack and Arbitrum also committing.
sections.body:
- EIP-8130 is planned for Base late September; OP Stack has committed to deploy later; Arbitrum has announced it will propose 8130 as its AA standard.
  - [Offchain Labs statement on 8141 & 8130](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2191#issuecomment-5411174429)
  - [Async video presentation by Chris](https://x.com/_chunter/status/2092236785329766404?s=20)
- Core thesis: Ethereum's existing EOA architecture already decouples authentication (ecrecover), authority (protocol-managed mapping), and account. EIP-8130 generalizes this one-to-one mapping into an updatable keystore contract.
- Key design elements:
  - Authenticator address is declared top-level in the transaction, making dependencies inspectable without tracing.
  - Keystore contract stores actor → authenticator mappings, updated via signed payloads; includes scopes and expiration.
  - 2D nonce (nonce key + nonce sequence) with a sentinel for non-sequential mode and a ring buffer for replay protection / expiry.
  - Call phases (2D array of atomic call batches) with committed phases guaranteeing call outcomes survive.
  - Account changes field covers 7702 delegation, keystore updates, and account creation.
  - Metadata field promoted to top-level (replaces appending calldata suffix).
- Chris argued the Frames (8141) account model "couples" execution, authentication, and authorization inside the account, forcing discovered (traced) dependencies rather than declared ones.
- Porting EIPs onto 8130: Recent roots become a sub-authenticator contract with no envelope change; post-quantum migration maps naturally because the keystore mapping can be updated from ecrecover to any contract-defined scheme.
- 8130 claimed advantages for statelessness: dependencies are bound to keystore and world state only; EIP-8369 (partial statelessness mitigation for Frames) would be unnecessary.
- Chris conceded one capability gap: Frames allows payment approval after execution (post-payment), which 8130 structurally cannot do because it precharges before execution.

sections.heading: Post-Payment Capability and Privacy Use Cases
sections.summary: Frames' ability to approve gas payment after execution is a real capability gap over 8130, but its practical impact is debated since it cannot work in the public mempool.
sections.body:
- Ben Adams raised that 8130's pre-charge model means a privacy withdrawal with no pre-existing payer cannot self-fund: the payer must have ETH before execution.
  - In Frames, consensus rules permit execution first and payment approval afterwards, though current public-mempool policy does not relay that shape.
  - [SimplePoolAuth example for 8130 permissionless gas payer](https://github.com/base/eip-8130-examples/blob/master/src/authenticators/gas-payers/SimplePoolAuth.sol)
- Chris conceded this is a genuine capability difference favoring Frames.
- Luca Donno (L2BEAT) argued the practical gap may be small: an ownerless, immutable paymaster contract (the privacy pool itself) can sponsor transactions under either model.
- Ben Adams raised potential legal implications: if the pool sponsors, responsibility may be attributed to the pool deployer rather than the individual transactor.
- Derek Chiang summarized: the question is whether post-payment capability justifies Frames' more complex validation model when it only works in private pools.
- Toni Wahrstätter noted that the privacy withdrawal use case does not necessarily require verify frames at arbitrary positions — a leading verify frame with the pool sponsoring and repayment inside verify may suffice.
  - [Excalidraw diagram from Luca Donno shared in chat]
- lightclient noted the non-public-mempool restriction is a DoS caution, not a hard consensus rule.

sections.heading: Discovered vs. Declared Dependencies and Mempool DoS
sections.summary: Debate centered on whether 8130's declared authenticator addresses meaningfully reduce mempool DoS risk compared to Frames' traced-dependency model.
sections.body:
- Felix (Geth) asked whether permissionless authenticator deployment in 8130 introduces similar DoS risks as Frames, since arbitrary authenticator code can still access state.
- Chris responded that 8130's decoupled architecture makes it easier to write pure-function authenticators; if recent roots are used, the protocol can track dependencies explicitly and the authenticator itself can remain stateless.
  - For stateful authenticators, 8130 falls back to trace rules identical to 8141.
- Ben Adams challenged that declaring only an authenticator address does not reveal what the code actually does; tracing is still needed for arbitrary authenticators.
- Chris acknowledged that fully stateful authenticators would require tracing, but argued the "dial" can be turned per chain profile (L2s may ban tracing; L1 may allow it).
- lightclient countered that both proposals are Turing complete and each can implement the other's logic; the practical difference is stylistic.
- Felix later clarified that Frames can enforce pure execution at runtime without requiring static pre-validation that code never accesses state — the code just cannot hit state during actual execution of the validation path.

sections.heading: L1/L2 Alignment and Process
sections.summary: Base signaled willingness to delay its 8130 fork to incorporate L1 feedback; participants agreed to timebox a collaboration attempt before accepting fragmentation.
sections.body:
- lightclient observed that 8130 is not CFI'd; EIP-8141 is the vehicle for native AA on L1 and is listed in [meta EIP-8081](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8081).
- Chris and Lumi (Offchain) clarified that "native AA" was CFI'd, not a specific EIP number.
- Chris stated Base would be happy to delay its fork to incorporate client-team feedback, though not indefinitely.
- Derek Chiang proposed a timeboxed collaboration: if 8141 and 8130 teams cannot converge on a shared spec within a few weeks, accept fragmentation and proceed separately.
  - Asked Chris to commit Base to not ship 8130 without going through this collaboration first; Chris reacted positively.
- Ansgar Dietrichs urged that L2 stakeholder interests be taken seriously — branching may not be inevitable and should not be treated as trivial.
- Mislav suggested the final spec should be built on top of 8141 but maintain full compatibility with 8130.
- lightclient emphasized EIP numbers are irrelevant; the design matters, and 8141's stylistic format already reflects what core devs find acceptable.
- spencer noted that future EIP proposals should follow the process in [EIP-7723](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7723), particularly the PFI section.

sections.heading: Enshrined Account Model vs. Protocol Primitives
sections.summary: Core devs from Nethermind, Geth, and ethrex expressed preference for providing generic primitives (Frames) rather than enshrining a specific account/keystore model.
sections.body:
- Pedro (WalletConnect) framed the core decision as whether the protocol should own the account model or provide primitives for wallets to own it, arguing wallet-level innovation on batching, sponsorship, and key rotation provides no competitive advantage and creates burden.
- lightclient asked client teams directly whether L1 should enshrine account-model logic.
- Stavros (Nethermind): Nethermind does not want to limit L1 to any specific account model; behavior should be generic, with market adapters deciding usage without requiring hard forks to change.
- Ben Adams (Nethermind): providing tools to create account systems is more important; enshrining a specific model puts account governance on ACDE indefinitely.
- Iván (ethrex): Frames implementation is not complex; arguments for 8130 are not convincing enough to switch; ethrex will announce two test networks (privacy-only with Frames + key nonsense + recent roots + FOCIL, and a Hegota-like playground with post-transaction assertions and native UTXOs).
- Mislav (ETH Labs): The divide between client teams and wallet/tooling teams is best served by Frames, with a separate governance track for a default (not reference) implementation that everyone uses — possibly maintained by a neutral consortium.
- Tomás (ethrex / Lambda): The EVM should support the lowest-level primitives possible; enshrining specific account models risks locking in decisions that are expensive to change.
- Felix (Geth): Not inherently against keystore functionality but it must be optional; a tried registry of schemes creates governance overhead; 8141's signature list already moves toward declaring supported schemes while preserving the escape hatch for user-defined ones.
- No client team spoke in favor of enshrining the 8130 account model or keystore on L1.

sections.heading: Signature Aggregation and Post-Quantum Considerations
sections.summary: Nico Consigny argued Frames' out-of-EVM typed signature list enables STARK aggregation of hash-based PQ signatures, which an enshrined authenticator set would complicate.
sections.body:
- Nicolas Consigny stated Frames was designed with a forward-syncing signature validated outside the EVM, enabling signature aggregation — the best known approach for L1 scaling.
  - STARK aggregation of SPHINCS+ / XMSS verifications amortizes thousands of PQ signature checks.
- He warned that an enshrined authenticator set creates a perpetual governance debate: the PQ landscape is shifting rapidly (lattice security boundaries moved due to the entropic attack), potentially requiring emergency hard forks.
  - Consigny was among the first to push lattice-based schemes (Falcon, ML-DSA precompiles) but now favors hash-based approaches at the protocol level.
- Chris countered that L1 could run fully permissionless authenticator deployment with whatever rules it wants, identical to 8141; the restricted canonical set is only for L2 admin keys.
- Consigny responded that removing deprecated non-PQ schemes would still generate political overhead.
- Chat discussion noted that 8130's authenticator model does not expose actorId in the tx envelope, which Toni Wahrstätter flagged as a problem for future signature aggregation; Pedro agreed it should be encoded as authenticator + actorId + data.

sections.heading: EIP-8130 Keystore as Companion EIP to Frames
sections.summary: Proposed next step: draft a companion EIP adding a keystore to Frames for L1/L2 account portability, without enshrining the full 8130 account model.
sections.body:
- lightclient stated the two main things 8130 adds are (1) enshrined wallet logic and (2) a different validation scheme with authenticators; L1 needs to decide on each independently.
- Derek Chiang proposed separating 8130's validation model (authenticator-based authentication) from its opinionated account features (actors, session keys, logs) and considering only the validation model for L1.
  - [Derek's writeup](https://x.com/decentrek/status/2092220720235565312)
- Sahi (Offchain Labs) advocated pushing more logic into signature frames and keeping stateful validation minimal; praised 8130's contract-address-based signature scheme identifiers as coordination-free.
  - Also mentioned the Guarantor mechanism: a party that fronts risk for the sequencer, allowing higher-gas-verification transactions.
  - Offchain Labs will create an EIP for the Guarantor mechanism; Pedro has started work at [EIP PR #11681](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11681).
- Felix suggested a companion EIP focused solely on the keystore, shared between L1 and L2, as a pragmatic path: even if transaction encodings differ, sharing keys preserves account portability.
  - Keystore updates invalidate only one transaction at a time, satisfying mempool DoS constraints.
- Toni Wahrstätter noted a keystore makes sense for a partial-stateful world anyway.
- lightclient: if someone wants to propose adding keystores to Frames, that is the obvious next step for evaluating whether this belongs on mainnet.
- Chris confirmed the keystore is a system contract; updating it would require a hard fork, but the mapping logic is very simple.

sections.heading: Next Steps
sections.summary: Key next step: someone drafts a companion EIP or proposal adding a keystore to Frames; further collaboration between 8141 and 8130 teams is timeboxed.
sections.body:
- lightclient proposed that someone draft a keystore addition to Frames (either integrated or as a companion EIP) as the most productive next step for evaluating the idea on mainnet.
- Felix endorsed a companion EIP focused solely on the keystore, allowing L1 and L2 to share key infrastructure even if transaction encodings differ.
- Derek Chiang urged timeboxing the 8141/8130 collaboration to a few weeks; if alignment is not reached, accept that L1 and L2s will diverge.
- Chris confirmed openness to delaying Base's 8130 fork to incorporate feedback.
- Offchain Labs committed to creating an EIP for the Guarantor mechanism.
- marc (moderator) noted the default path remains 8141 proceeding on mainnet and 8130 on L2s, with this call serving to surface what small or large tweaks to 8141 could meaningfully improve cross-chain outcomes.
- Next scheduled touchpoint: ACDE on Thursday.
